explanation.surface: A note about a larder: preserves and jams.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickles are vinegar-preserved foods, and pickles are also tight spots, the way jams are awkward predicaments.

parts.note: a mine is a pit dug for coal
fall is the American word for autumn

explanation.surface: A warning about an unseen mine that will be dug before the autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap dug and covered over is an unseen hazard, and the word now means any unsuspected snag.

clue.text: Freeing Victoria, for example, the wounded went through it

parts.note: clearing a path means freeing it of obstacles
Victoria is a major London railway station

explanation.surface: Someone frees a woman named Victoria while casualties pass through.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria looks like a person's name; it is the London terminus, an example of a station.
explanation.definitionFit: A field medical post behind the front line sorted injured soldiers before sending them back for treatment.

clue.text: Long-boat for pairs what a frolic!

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for long, as in longitude
Noah's ark took the animals on board two by two

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims with delight at a long rowing boat built for crews of two.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boat for pairs' suggests a rowing double; it is Noah's vessel, boarded two by two.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit of fun or a carefree escapade is a synonym of a playful romp.

indicators.note: from says the bunk is made out of the settee, so the settee's word comes first

parts.note: a chesterfield is a padded leather settee
a bunk is a narrow bed

explanation.surface: A question about whether a bunk could come from a Chesterfield.
explanation.walkthrough: Chesterfield looks like the English town; it is the buttoned leather settee, and a settee that becomes a bed is the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A settee that unfolds into somewhere to sleep is a bunk derived from the couch.

indicators.note: the young man sits inside the word for agony, as the clue's in says

parts.note: agony means pain
a lad is a young man

explanation.surface: A wandering knight finds a young man in agony.
explanation.definitionFit: A wandering champion of chivalry, originally one of Charlemagne's twelve peers.

indicators.note: planned suggests the letters are laid out to a new design, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: A road crossing is put in at a planned site.
explanation.walkthrough: A PELICAN crossing is a British pedestrian crossing with push-button traffic lights.
explanation.definitionFit: A light-controlled pedestrian crossing in Britain takes its name from a bird.

clue.text: Jemmy is one that turns to provide swag

indicators.note: turns tells us to read the word for the jemmy backwards

parts.note: a jemmy is a burglar's crowbar, a tool

explanation.surface: A burglar's jemmy is used to force things and so produce stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Swag is stolen goods, plunder carried off by thieves.

indicators.note: perhaps hints the letters may be arranged otherwise, an anagram signal
endlessly removes the final letter of the word permutate

explanation.surface: A machine boasting it would shuffle logic without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the last E of PERMUTATE, and 'perhaps' rearranges LOGICID plus PERMUTAT; the whole clue also describes the machine.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic calculating machine works by tirelessly processing logical operations.

parts.note: toddlers play in a children's room, and in horse racing a handicap race is run only by juvenile horses

explanation.surface: Toddlers run about in a playroom.
explanation.walkthrough: In British racing a nursery is a handicap for two-year-old horses, so 'run' is a race as well as toddling.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a room or school for small children and a flat race restricted to juvenile horses.

clue.text: Lad for gutter, he'd appear in novel form

definitions.text: Lad for gutter, he'd appear in novel form

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters appear in a new form, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: A street urchin destined for the gutter turns up in a work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' is both the anagram signal (new) and Dickens's Oliver Twist, where the pickpocket boy appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Dawkins, Fagin's young pickpocket in Oliver Twist, is a street boy in a novel.

clue.text: Invisible emanation from a uranium source

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the words a uranium

explanation.surface: Radiation given off by a uranium source cannot be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'source' completes the surface picture of radioactive material and supplies no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A subtle atmosphere or glow thought to surround a person or thing.

parts.note: reads like the counter at a Chinese food shop, but means bead frames used in China to do subtraction, or take away

explanation.surface: The serving counters in a Chinese food shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Bead frames, plural of abacus, are traditional Chinese calculating devices used for sums such as subtraction.

parts.note: blinking is a mild British swear word, but here literally means when you blink, as with a sore eyelid swelling

explanation.surface: Something that is blooming painful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blinking' is a mild British intensifier like 'bloody'; here it means shutting the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflamed swelling on the eyelid hurts each time the eye closes.

clue.text: It is commonplace putting curse on a learner-driver

parts.note: a ban is an old word for a curse or anathema
L is the plate displayed by a British learner driver

explanation.surface: Swearing at a learner driver is an ordinary thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the curse above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Trite and ordinary, lacking any originality.

clue.text: When mouse runs down, make reparation

explanation.surface: When the mouse runs down the clock, someone makes amends.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Hickory Dickory Dock, 'the clock struck one, the mouse ran down': at one o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the mouse ran down at one o'clock; and to make amends for a wrong is to expiate it.

clue.text: Beamset back in ground and rope about the neck

indicators.note: in places the turned beam inside the word for ground

parts.note: ground means land

indicators.note: set back tells us the word for beam is turned round

parts.note: a beam of light is a ray

explanation.surface: A beam is reset in the ground, and a rope is slung round someone's neck.
explanation.walkthrough: The page runs 'Beam set' together as one word; 'set back' is the reversal signal and 'and' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord worn round the neck to carry a whistle, knife or pass.

parts.note: looks like leisure outside a law court, but means tennis played close up at the front of the court

explanation.surface: People relax outside the court building.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, volleying close to the mesh at the front of the court is a style of play.

clue.text: Body of people grow old there's the rub!

parts.note: a mass is a large body of people
to age is to grow old

explanation.surface: A crowd of people ageing, with Hamlet's line about the difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there's the rub' is Hamlet's phrase for a snag; here rub is a physical rubdown.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubdown kneading the muscles is a soothing treatment.

clue.text: Dignity-that is a joke in my embrace

indicators.note: embrace means the word my wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: taken as written
a jest is a joke

explanation.surface: Dignity held close in my arms is no laughing matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Stately grandeur or regal bearing.

clue.text: Old instruments of torture, these locomotives

explanation.surface: The locomotives are compared to old torture devices.
explanation.definitionFit: In old usage an engine was any contrivance, including a rack; and railway locomotives are engines.

parts.note: looks like making a plane take off, but means a referee ordering a player from the football pitch

explanation.surface: Something makes an aircraft lift off.
explanation.walkthrough: In football a referee dismisses a player from the field for a serious foul.
explanation.definitionFit: A referee dismissing a player makes them leave the pitch.

parts.note: Frank looks like a man's name, but to frank a letter is to mark it with postage, and such a mark is pressed into the paper

explanation.surface: A man called Frank was impressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Franked mail bears postage marks, and pressing a design into something marks it in.

clue.text: But broker could buy them as presents

definitions.text: But broker could buy them as presents

parts.words: But broker could buy them as presents
parts.note: presents look like gifts, but the joke is the opposite of the present tense: contracts for goods delivered at a later date

explanation.surface: A stockbroker might buy these as gifts.
explanation.definitionFit: Contracts to trade commodities at a set later date are traded by brokers, and what lies ahead is the opposite of the present.

clue.text: Shaw's maid, little woman with a short name

parts.note: Jo March is one of the sisters in Little Women
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Shaw's maid is described as a little woman with a brief name.
explanation.walkthrough: Bernard Shaw's play Saint Joan is about the Maid of Orleans.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's play Saint Joan portrays the Maid of Orleans.

indicators.note: around suggests the letters are moved about, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: Ancient carved letters found near the Northern Irish town of Omagh.
explanation.walkthrough: Omagh is a town in Northern Ireland, fitting the old Irish script.
explanation.definitionFit: An early medieval Irish alphabet of strokes carved on stones.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Starting price — it makes you !' with no count and the word after 'you' missing; SP + IT gives the letters but the definition is lost and no search found the full text.

clue.text: Bonnie Prince Charlie's refuge-heavens! English close behind

indicators.note: close behind places the English letter right after the word for heavens

parts.note: the heavens are the sky

explanation.surface: Fleeing to Skye, the prince exclaims as the English close in behind.
explanation.walkthrough: After Culloden in 1746 Charles Edward Stuart escaped to the Hebridean island of Skye.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebridean island where the fugitive Stuart prince hid in 1746.

explanation.surface: Someone is tempted to cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: A slope is inclined; and in British slang a racket or con is a swindle.

explanation.surface: A strong plasterer's job described.
explanation.walkthrough: Sticking plaster is also British for an adhesive bandage, strapping for a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: Applying render to walls is a plasterer's job; and an adhesive dressing is a sort of strapping.

indicators.note: to become suggests the letters change into something new, an anagram signal

explanation.surface: Keen people hoping to turn into baseball players.
explanation.definitionFit: The New York team are famous baseball professionals.

indicators.note: in tells us the king's letter goes inside the word for warehouses

parts.note: depots are warehouses
R is the abbreviation for king, from Rex

explanation.surface: Exiled royalty kept in storage buildings.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel someone from a country is to banish them.
